standard.title: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights
standard.description: the origins and significance of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, including Australia's involvement in the development of the declaration
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have studied significant international agreements and declarations prior to WWII, including the League of Nations and the context of interwar international law.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students describe the origins and significance of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, explain Australia's involvement in its development, and investigate its present significance.

nodes.label: Origins and Australia's role
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe the causes of the development of the UDHR and explain Australia's involvement in its drafting.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe at least two causes of the UDHR's development and explain the role Australia played in its drafting.
nodes.typical_width: Describe the causes of the UDHR's development — the atrocities of the Holocaust, the immense scale of destruction and displacement caused by the Second World War, the failure of the pre-war international legal order to prevent genocide — explaining why these events made a new international human rights framework necessary; explain Australia's involvement including the roles of HV Evatt (President of the UN General Assembly when the UDHR was adopted) and Jessie Street in drafting the declaration.
wider: Examine the drafting debates that shaped the UDHR — investigating which rights were contested (e.g. economic and social rights vs civil and political rights) and what the negotiations reveal about the political context of 1948

Investigate Jessie Street's advocacy for women's rights in the UDHR drafting process, examining how her work contributed to the document's gender equality provisions and how her contribution has been historically recognised

response_modes.reason: The UDHR's origins are directly caused by the Holocaust and WWII — make this causal link explicit. Students who have studied K03 (Holocaust) should be able to construct the causal argument themselves: 'The Holocaust demonstrated that X, therefore the UDHR was designed to ensure Y.'

success_criteria: Describe at least two causes of the development of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights
Explain Australia's involvement in drafting the UDHR, naming at least one individual and their contribution
Connect the origins of the UDHR to specific events of the Second World War studied earlier in the course

nodes.label: Present significance
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can investigate the present significance of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights as a living international instrument.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain at least two ways the UDHR remains significant today.
nodes.typical_width: Investigate the present significance of the UDHR as a living instrument: its influence on subsequent international law (covenants, conventions, UNDRIP), its use in domestic courts and policy debates, its invocation by civil rights movements (including First Nations campaigns in Australia), and ongoing debates about which rights it protects and how they should be enforced.
wider: Investigate how the UDHR has been invoked in First Nations Australians' rights campaigns, examining the relationship between universal human rights principles and the specific rights claims of First Peoples — including the development of UNDRIP as a more targeted instrument
Examine a specific contemporary human rights case or campaign that invokes the UDHR, analysing how the document is used as both a legal reference and a moral argument

response_modes.reason: This node integrates K15's origins story with the civil rights themes of K09–K13 — the UDHR's present significance is most clearly seen in its application to the rights of First Nations Australians, women, and migrants examined throughout the course.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The UDHR's application to First Nations rights (including UNDRIP) connects directly to K09–K13, making this a productive integration point for the course's civil rights themes. Students can examine how universal rights principles interact with specific group rights claims.
success_criteria: Explain at least two ways the Universal Declaration of Human Rights remains significant today
Describe how the UDHR has influenced subsequent international law or domestic policy
Explain the connection between the UDHR and the rights campaigns of First Nations Australians, women, or migrants studied earlier in the course
nodes.notes: Limited width descriptor — only two elaborations. Both are used across Nodes 1 and 2. Wider items deepen the analysis within the same document's origins and significance rather than adding new phenomena.
